data.title: Slotkin slams US attorney probing lawmakers as stunt for 'publicity and your political ambitions'
data.description:
Rep. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) on Wednesday fired back at the Texas-based U.S. attorney who penned letters threatening to investigate her and four other lawmakers, saying Aaron Reitz’s correspondence “is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz wrote to Slotkin last week, posting the letter to X and writing that comments she made about oversight investigations sending a deterrence message “sounds potentially illegal to me.”

Slotkin responded late Wednesday with a video and letter of her own, noting she has Speech and Debate Clause protections, calling his investigation “baseless” and saying he should “withdraw your letter immediately.”

“Your threats to prosecute a sitting senator for speech and legislative oversight also violate Justice Department policy. Your breach of these rules — publicly posting your letter instead of providing it directly to me, my attorney, or Senate Legal Counsel, is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry,” she wrote.

“Exercising the power of a U.S. Attorney because you do not like my ‘political association, activities, or beliefs’ is also prohibited by the Justice Manual — and more importantly by the First Amendment and by the very criminal laws you mistakenly cited in your threat. As a United States Senator, I preserve my records as a matter of course. I have no intent of changing that practice now.”

Reitz’s letter cited comments from Slotkin noting that President Trump’s associates do not carry the immunity bestowed on the executive and saying investigating malfeasance of the administration could send a “deterrence message” to those interested in working in the Trump White House.

In her video message, Slotkin said she was being targeted “because I said aloud in a podcast that if you violate the law or waste taxpayer dollars, you should be held accountable.”

Alongside Slotkin, Reitz has sent letters to Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). He also sent a letter to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), similarly demanding he preserve his records. In each, he has argued Democrats could be violating the law through their investigations.

Schiff, the latest recipient of a letter from Reitz, also responded Wednesday. 

“No amount of bluster by this Justice Department will stop my efforts to expose the corruption and abuse of power at the heart of this administration,” he wrote on X.

“The American people demanded accountability and they will have it. I won’t back down. I won’t be intimidated. I have all the authority I need. It’s called Article I of the Constitution,” he added, citing the portion of the Constitution creating Congress.

In conducting widespread firings, the White House has repeatedly cited Trump’s Article II authority, the section that establishes the presidency.

Slotkin ended her letter by suggesting she may have an additional response to Reitz.

“I reserve all rights to take appropriate actions in the future as it relates to this sham investigation,” she wrote.

data.title: Trump says people stockpiling food, water amid outages should 'relax'
data.description:
President Trump on Wednesday said that Americans purchasing and stockpiling canned food and water in response to the recent series of major outages should all “relax” and that “everything’s good.”

Trump downplayed concerns over these outages in an interview with Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich in Shenzen, China, saying that they were all “individual events. She later asked again about people stocking up on goods in the event of a larger outage.

“Tell them to relax, everything’s good,” he replied. “These are individual events.”

He added that if these incidents happened under former President Biden, “which was grossly incompetent and corrupt, nobody would have mentioned it.”

“These are not –– I’ll let you know if there’s a problem,” Trump said.

The president noted that these outages have happened after “putting in new equipment,” as outages with Apple and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) were both said to be connected to upgrades to their systems.

He emphasized the need for funding to refurbish the FAA’s digital infrastructure, and he said that all funding should not be spent “until we can do the whole thing, the whole system.”

“You don’t want to do piecemeal,” he said. “That’s what they did before –– I build, I build very well. I made a lot of money building things, always, and I know how to do this stuff, And I said, ‘Don’t.'”

He later said that the country will have the “best system anywhere in the world. Air traffic control, it’s called.”

Trump previously evaluated the outages when asked about them on Tuesday, telling reporters “it’s fine.”

Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on Monday similarly asked Vice President Vance if Americans should stock up on food and water after countries in Europe made similar requests to their citizens.

“A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance replied. “My answer to that is no. We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything.”

Americans have seen a wave of outages affecting companies like Microsoft, Apple, and United Airlines, along with disruptions accessing J.P. Morgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo accounts. But facets of the federal government, specifically the FAA and the National Security Agency (NSA), have also been affected by downed systems.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop of all flights, the third in the last 25 years, last Thursday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it was likely due to a router being updated from copper-wiring to fiber optics at a radio post in Arkansas.

Trump told Heinrich that Duffy was “doing fantastic.”

Administration officials have also dismissed that any of these incidents were caused by cyberattacks or rogue AI. But Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that super intelligence (SI), the Trump administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence, could have been behind the recent outages.

data.title: Elbridge Colby chides Ukraine's strikes inside Russia, drawing German rebuke
data.description:
Elbridge Colby, U.S. under secretary of defense, criticized Ukraine for its long-range strikes against Russia, drawing rebuke from allies during high-level talks at NATO headquarters on Tuesday.

Colby said that strikes “have not been effective … nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.” He also added that they “have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve.”

NATO allies, in response, stepped up for Kyiv during the Ukrainian Defence Contact Group meeting. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Colby’s criticism was “quite a stupid thing” and that the focus should instead be on Russia’s strikes.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he believed the long-range strikes were helpful. “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” he added.

Per The Telegraph, Colby walked out of the meeting without hearing a classified war briefing from Ukraine’s defense minister.

Kyiv has ramped up its long-range attacks on Russia in recent months. On Tuesday, Ukraine struck the Kremlin’s Kerch Bridge, which links Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula. 

Domestically-developed drones struck the bridge’s road section, and missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media following the attacks.

The strike demonstrated Ukraine’s diverse homemade weapons after facing munition shortages provided by the U.S. and Europe. Some attacks in recent months have utilized more than 1,000 drones.

data.title: Social Security raise: What's left after the Medicare premium hike?
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Retirees are getting their biggest Social Security cost-of-living increase in four years, but higher Medicare Part B premiums will eat up some of that raise.

The standard Part B premium is rising $6.50 a month in 2027, which will trim the average Social Security bump from $75 to roughly $68.50 a month for retirees who have it deducted from their checks.

Put another way, the Part B premium hike will absorb about 9% of the $75 boost.

That’s good news for retirees after what happened this year, when a nearly $18 jump in the Part B premium ate into almost a third of the average Social Security raise.

But those figures are based on the average benefit. For retirees with smaller Social Security checks, the same Part B hike will take a bigger chunk out of their cost-of-living bump.

What the Part B hike means for your Social Security check

Social Security recipients are getting a 3.6% cost-of-living boost in January, which will raise the average benefit for retired workers by about $75 to $2,170 a month, according to the Social Security Administration.

The standard Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, so a retiree receiving the average benefit is left with roughly $1,960 after it’s deducted.

But many retirees get much smaller checks, and for those who have the premium withheld, the same $6.50 hike will consume a larger share of their raise.

Social Security increase before and after the Part B hike in 2027

Federal data shows more than 5.7 million retired workers received less than $1,000 a month in Social Security benefits in June.

For those getting $1,000 a month, the 3.6% COLA for 2027 will add $36, meaning the Part B increase will absorb about 18% of that raise.

If the premium goes up more than a retiree’s raise, the federal “hold harmless” rule can keep their Social Security check from shrinking, though that’s not expected to apply to many people next year.

Some Medicare Part B enrollees, around 9%, also pay a surcharge on top of the standard premium if their income is above a certain level. Those income thresholds for 2027 are listed here.

data.title: Begich holds Alaska's lone House seat for GOP
data.description:
Republican Rep. Nick Begich is projected to win a second term in Alaska’s at-large House district, according to Decision Desk HQ. 

Begich beat out independent Bill Hill, who was backed by Democrats, as well as Democrat Eric Hafner and Libertarian James McDermott in the four-way general election showdown. 

Democrat Matt Schultz suspended his campaign ahead of the primary, warning that “democracy itself is under threat” and calling on his supporters to back Hill. 

After Begich and Hill advanced from this summer’s top-four, nonpartisan primary, Alaska’s Democratic Party also endorsed the independent over Hafner, who reportedly has no ties to the state and is incarcerated in New York. 

Alaska is considered a solidly red state, but it’s also shown an openness to independents and moderate Democrats. Independent Bill Walker was elected governor in 2014, and Democrat Mary Peltola won the Last Frontier’s lone House seat in a 2022 special election before securing a full term.

The Republican clinched 51.35 percent of the vote over Hill’s 48.65, DDHQ projected Wednesday night just before 9:30 p.m. EST.

Begich won the seat for Republicans in 2024, ousting Peltola, who beat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan for the Senate seat in this year’s midterms.

data.title: Trump says 'we'll wipe them out' if Iran dirty bombs US
data.description:
President Trump on Wednesday renewed his threat to annihilate Iran if it goes forward with its reported threat to launch a dirty bomb on U.S. soil.

Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich asked Trump while in Shenzen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit if Washington, D.C., residents should worry about Iran launching a dirty bomb on the city.

“I don’t think so, no,” he said. “I mean, look, if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.”

The president said there was a “huge indication” that Iran has been “looking at gases, looking at bio,” referring to biological weapons, to attack the U.S. He said that using nuclear weapons “is much harder.”

“You know, these are nasty people,” Trump said. “We didn’t start this war. This was was started 51 years ago … you look at the USS Cole, where 400 of our kids were killed.”

The president previously said on Tuesday that he took the threat of the dirty bomb from Iran “very seriously” because “they happen to be crazy,” and he warned that the Islamic regime will “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before.”

The alleged plot was reported by CNN and other outlets and suggested that U.S. intelligence indicates that Iran is developing plans to target senior administration officials by setting off a dirty bomb.

Some Trump administration officials have noted that threats from Iran have “substantially increased” and that the U.S. and its service members abroad “are under greater threat,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers Wednesday. 

Other officials have downplayed the CNN report. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that “the homeland is secure,” and that there was no “new threat” from Iran’s “aspirational” planning.

Iranian officials have pushed back against the reporting. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the allegations “baseless” and a “fabricated media narrative” in a post on social platform X. 

“RUBBISH. Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it. Nobody is buying it,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the reporting in an X post.

The U.S. is seen as particularly vulnerable to a dirty bomb attack. The weapon uses conventional explosives with radioactive material to contaminate the area and affect as many people in a dense urban area as possible. Washington is home to 700,000 people and brings in tens of thousands more who commute to work daily.

While a dirty bomb, also known as a “radiological dispersal device” (RDD), is considered far, far less damaging than a conventional nuclear bomb, the explosion of such a weapon could cause death or injury to anyone within the blast radius.

data.title: Musk on midterms spending: 'I feel pretty foolish'
data.description:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Wednesday said he feels “pretty foolish” after he spent $442 million toward Republican campaigns in the 2026 midterm elections, where the party saw sweeping losses to Democrats.

Musk, the world’s richest person, told New York Times columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin virtually at the DealBook Summit that his goal was to have Republicans keep control of the Senate. Democrats won a majority and claimed another victory after Democrat Mary Peltola won her Senate race in Alaska, giving the party 56 seats to the GOP’s 44.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money. Obviously you can put a lot of money into an election and have an effect that is relatively minor, and I think that was the case here.”

“So probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money, and I didn’t put a lot of personal attention into it because I’m focused on building SpaceX, Tesla,” he added.

He later said that his motivation was to have the House, Senate or the White House be controlled by Republicans going into 2029, though he said he did not want either a “supermajority” of Democrats or Republicans.

“I think we have some want to have some checks and balances here,” Musk said. “And that was it, really. So, you know, I think I’m ideologically quite moderate. I don’t think I like, you know, any kind of extreme political views.”

Musk said in the interview that he’s “not MAGA” and that he was not sure what it means, “but if that means, sort of, blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

This stark admission follows Musk’s previous close relationship with President Trump in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election and subsequent hiring as the head of the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

How the two operated prompted some critics to claim they ran a “co-presidency,” though the two feuded before Musk eventually left his role to focus on his companies and DOGE shut down in July after its executive order mandate expired.

In October 2024, Musk said he was “dark gothic MAGA” during a Trump rally at Madison Square Garden, wearing a black MAGA hat with a font criticized as resembling the font Fraktur, which the Nazis used during their reign in Germany. Experts have since debunked this.

Musk has championed other right-wing political parties globally. He notably appeared virtually at a rally in January 2025 for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. The party’s landslide victory in the German state Saxony-Anhalt last month was described by Georgetown University researchers as opening “the possibility of Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi era.”

data.title: DOJ charges Russian national with spying on workers for 'large' defense tech company
data.description:
Federal prosecutors charged a Russian national with secretly working for Moscow to conduct illegal surveillance of employees at a major defense technology company over Ukraine’s use of its technology in the war against Russia, the Justice Department announced Wednesday.

Igor D’iu, who was arrested Oct. 30, allegedly followed workers, tracked down their home addresses and used fake identification documents to gather information about the technology giant and its employees as part of a Russian-directed operation.

The Justice Department did not directly identify the company by name in its announcement, but Bloomberg News identified the company as Palantir, citing a source familiar with the matter.

“The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said in a statement.

According to the department, D’iu entered the U.S. illegally over the summer through the U.S. Mexico border after being recruited through the messaging platform Telegram. Prosecutors said his handlers provided him with money, equipment and instructions to carry out surveillance near the company’s Palo Alto offices.

His assignments initially involved visiting designated locations before allegedly expanding to photographing employees’ laptop screens at a nearby coffee shop and following workers home.

He was instructed to position a laptop near the company’s offices so his contacts could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from employees in the area, according to the DOJ. His handlers also allegedly told him to target the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.

During an October search of his East Palo Alto residence, FBI agents found approximately $18,000 in cash, two Russian passports, electronic equipment and a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, many of which matched the homes of company employees.

“Igor D’iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major U.S. technology company,” Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.

Palatnir, which provides software to U.S. intelligence agencies and military forces, has played a significant role in supporting Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Palantir CEO Alex Karp traveled to Kyiv that same year, where he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

data.title: Cornyn blocks Trump's nomination to federal district court because he didn't choose a Texan
data.description:
Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Wednesday blocked President Trump’s judicial nominee T. Elliot Gaiser from being confirmed for a seat on the U.S. District Court in the Northern District of Texas because the nominee is not from Texas.

Cornyn, the outgoing senator to be succeeded by Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), did not submit a blue slip for Gaiser. This process is a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition where the chair asks home-state senators to assess the nominee. If withheld or returned with rejections, the process does not generally move forward.

A Cornyn aide told The Hill’s The Gavel that he instead pushed the White House for months to recommend Steve Fahey, a former federal prosecutor, for the vacancy. Cornyn accused the White House of having “completely ignored” his requests and said he was “not willing to let the White House ignore the Senate’s constitutional role.”

Gaiser was expected to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee for a confirmation hearing on Wednesday but was not among the seven candidates for federal judgeships to testify.

“I just refuse to be jammed by a non-Texan who has no trial experience, who hasn’t been vetted,” Cornyn told CNN. “And so, we provided the White House an alternative, and I’m hoping they take advantage of it because I don’t want the seat to go vacant either.”

Cornyn told CBS News that Gaiser’s nomination was “no longer viable.”

“He’s not a Texan, has no trial experience, and the White House tried to jam the Senate and wouldn’t allow us to do our due diligence that we need to do on lifetime appointments,” he told the outlet.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Gaiser lived in Ohio before he was tapped to lead the Office of Legal Counsel at the Department of Justice. Trump formally sent Gaiser’s nomination on Monday.

Gaiser issued a classified legal opinion justifying lethal strikes against drug cartels and suspected drug traffickers, CNN reported last month. He said that the strikes did not trigger the war powers law due to not meeting the definition of “hostilities,” the network added.

The Ohioan also ruled in August that Trump’s outside advisers are protected from any future congressional and legal investigations, with internal communications with these outside advisers protected by executive privilege.

Other lame duck Republican lawmakers have indicated that other judicial nominees could face roadblocks to their confirmation, including Trump’s choice for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma, attorney Zach West. Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.) withdrew his support for West, while Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said he may not drop his opposition.

“Frankly, it’s an unforced error by the White House just not to consult more effectively with Senator Armstrong,” Tillis told Bloomberg. “I think he’ll get done, but they’re running it down to the wire.”

data.title: Iran's 'dirty bomb' threat underscores risks to US homeland
data.description:
A reported plot by Iran to target Washington, D.C., with a so-called “dirty bomb” has brought fears of an attack on the U.S. homeland to the forefront this week.

Coming on the heels of two men arrested late last month for a suspected Iran-linked terror plot on a U.S.-run airbase in the United Kingdom, experts say Iran appears to be looking for options to impose costs on the U.S. as President Trump’s war on the country stretches on.

“These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers Wednesday of Iran, during a House worldwide threats hearing. 

Other officials have downplayed the CNN report, which cited intelligence that Iran was planning to target senior Trump administration officials using materials already in the U.S. 

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that “the homeland is secure,” and Iran’s planning was “aspirational” and not a “new threat.”

Speaking during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Clayton would not comment on CNN’s reporting, only saying that the U.S. remains committed “to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States.”

Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues, said America has “been worried about the threat of a dirty bomb in a major metropolitan U.S. city” since before the 9/11 attacks.

“In that sense, there’s nothing new about the threat,” Haggerty, who is now with the Defense Priorities think tank, told The Hill.

And since the first Trump administration, Iran has plotted against current and former U.S. officials — most plans concentrated on attacking individuals while they were traveling overseas — including a murder-for-hire plot against Trump himself in 2024.

But Haggerty noted that Tehran is “looking for options right now” to impose costs on the U.S. to make it harder for Washington to continue a blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, a military operation that has crippled Tehran’s economy and has been in place since summer. The wider war is now nearing the nine-month mark. 

“They don’t want to return to full-scale war right now. That’s not what they’re looking to do,” he said. “An attack like a dirty bomb on U.S. soil . . . it would really have to be in response to something much more threatening to Tehran to warrant something like that.” 

Instead, “they’re looking in other domains. It’s called horizontal escalation,” Haggerty added. “Iran can’t outdo us militarily. But maybe in a different domain like cyber or assassination or something like that, they can strike us in this other area to impose greater costs and make it harder for us to continue on our current trajectory of holding the blockade.” 

These asymmetrical threats impose a cost on the U.S. simply by forcing the government and military to increase measures to guard against such a scenario.

Case in point, CNN reported that the dirty bomb plotting picked up by U.S. intelligence, which included very specific locations and targets, set off a flurry of contingency planning in Washington.

Other intelligence suggesting Tehran may use chemical weapons against U.S. service members, diplomatic and intelligence personnel stationed in the Middle East reportedly prompted a separate planning effort to make sure Americans there have the necessary equipment and training to protect themselves.

And the U.S. was forced to quickly move its aircraft from two airfields in the U.K. after five men were initially arrested on Sept. 27 for a suspected terror plot on the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, England.

American B-1 bombers positioned at RAF Fairford to strike Iran were moved in October.

Another 13 American aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall were spotted departing for bases elsewhere in Europe earlier this month due to a threat related to Iran, The Wall Street Journal first reported.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the time that the United States is “constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons.”

The longer the Iran war stretches, the greater the chance that such threats escalate, according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

“A prolonged war heightens the prospects for all types of escalation — cyber, assassinations, drones and other asymmetric capabilities,” she told The Hill. “We’ve already seen increased reporting of Iranian intent/desire to undertake such attacks, for example on U.S. fighter jets at UK military bases.” 

But she was in a similar mindset as Haggerty that Iran’s intent is not necessarily to provoke wider war. 

“A ‘dirty bomb’ in the U.S. would signal a significant uptick in Iranian capabilities, which seems unlikely at this time,” Yacoubian said.
